articles.title: NBA Europe: London and Manchester bid race heats up as crunch meetings take place in New York around World Cup final
articles.summary: NBA chiefs will hold talks with prospective NBA Europe owners in New York this weekend; London is reportedly the most sought-after franchise destination with highest-value bids; Manchester is also one of the target cities, with the league scheduled to start in October 2027
articles.body:
NBA Commissioner Adam Silver and Deputy Commissioner Mark Tatum will be speaking to bidders in town ahead of Sunday's World Cup final at MetLife Stadium.

Some of the top capital investment firms in the world are in the US metropolis for the showpiece and Silver intends to make the most of it with a view to shaping the deals for the first franchises, which are expected to drop in the coming weeks and months heading into the autumn.

"We've had tremendous interest from multiple cities in Europe, including cities that we didn't even ask for bids from," Silver said after the NBA's Board of Governors meeting in Las Vegas earlier this week.

"We discussed with our board today that we're in the process of finalising those bids, I think for an initial group of cities. Many of the people who are involved in those bids, the European bidders, are actually going to be in New York for the World Cup final on Sunday.

"Mark and I are going to be attending several meetings with them, given their presence in New York. I would say we're hoping to wrap up some of those deals over the next several weeks and then announcements will be forthcoming."

London is very much at the centre of the bidding race and is reported to be the most heavily contested market with multiple bids topping $1bn, Sky Sports understands.

Sky News has reported that Liberty Global, the majority shareholder of Formula E, tabled an offer for the London franchise and that former Tottenham Hotspur executive chairman Daniel Levy has joined a consortium being assembled with Jahm Najafi, the MSP Sports Capital co-founder.

Sky News also reported that the Reuben family, who hold a stake in Newcastle United, are among the suitors for the London team.

The Athletic reported that Buss Sports Capital - the investment group founded by members of the family who previously owned the Los Angeles Lakers - has bid in several cities, including London, Manchester and Lyon.

Overall, more than 20 groups submitted finalised bids by the end of June, with viable offers in all 12 target cities and multiple bids in the 10-figure range in select markets. City AM has reported that Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Chelsea co-owner Todd Boehly were among those credited with interest in London, the most sought-after franchise of all and the market with the most valuable committed bids, reportedly multiple above $1bn.

George Aivazoglou, the NBA's managing director for Europe and the Middle East, told Sky Sports : "We're extremely encouraged by the level of interest in the NBA and FIBA's proposed league in Europe, including from existing basketball and football clubs, outside investors, prospective commercial and media partners, federations, domestic leagues and, most importantly, fans.

"In addition to preserving and celebrating Europe's rich basketball traditions and passionate fanbases, we're particularly excited about the opportunity to bring permanent, world-class basketball to marquee European cities like London and Manchester here in the UK, where basketball fandom and participation are at an all-time high."

What is NBA Europe and what do we know about it?

NBA Europe is the creation of a new professional basketball league with the NBA working in partnership with FIBA, the sport's global governing body.

They are targeting an October 2027 launch - which Adam Silver said last month is very much "on schedule" - and barring an unlikely alliance it will act as a direct challenge to the existing EuroLeague at the top of the European club game. The plan is for 16 teams, 12 of which will be permanent franchises, plus four places earned each year on merit through FIBA competition.

Twelve cities have been targeted for the permanent franchises, London and Manchester, Paris and Lyon, Madrid and Barcelona, Milan and Rome, Berlin and Munich, plus Istanbul and Athens.

The NBA is looking to tap into the European fan culture which left NBA stars very impressed on their most recent European sojourn.

The first owners will be known soon, with announcements to follow and an expectation that the first NBA Europe teams will be unveiled by early autumn.

articles.title: New York Knicks' OG Anunoby returns to London to inspire next generation after playing pivotal role in NBA Finals victory
articles.summary: OG Anunoby produced iconic late score to win Game 4 in NBA Finals series against San Antonio Spurs; London-born star went on to help Knicks win first championship in 53 years; Anunoby tells Sky Sports about his playoff heroics, growing basketball in Britain and his love for Arsenal
articles.body:
Born in Harlesden, Anunoby arrives home with his second NBA title. But this time it is different.

Unlike his first title with the Toronto Raptors in 2019, when injury prevented him from featuring in the playoff run, this time Anunoby played a defining role, delivering one of the NBA Finals' most memorable moments.

Trailing by 29 points in Game 4 against the San Antonio Spurs, the Knicks looked set to give up control of the series before completing the largest comeback in NBA Finals history.

With seconds remaining and Madison Square Garden on the edge of their seats, Anunoby acted, tipping home what proved to be the winning basket with just 1.2 seconds remaining, leading them to victory by just one point.

The Knicks enjoyed a fairy-tale run to the Finals but still entered the showdown with Victor Wembanyama's San Antonio Spurs as underdogs as they looked to end a 53-year wait for a championship.

Yet inside the locker room there was always belief, as Anunoby explained to Sky Sports . "Honestly, before the start of the playoffs, our whole team just came together and we knew we had one goal. We took every game day by day, game by game," he said.

"We went on a crazy run. I don't know how many games we won in a row (13) but every game was focused on the next, trying to build and be better than we were the last game.

"Even in the Finals, it was just day by day, game by game."

The Knicks' remarkable winning run that propelled them through the playoffs was finally ended in Game 3 by the Spurs. Their momentum looked to have evaporated after three quarters of Game 4, with San Antonio on the brink of levelling the series.

The Knicks finally rallied before Anunoby produced the defining moment of the Finals. But while the rest of basketball continues to replay the moment, Anunoby has already moved on.

"It comes up quite a bit so I see it quite a bit." Does he still get the same feeling every time he watches it back?

It is a typically understated response from Anunoby. Even immediately after Game 4, amid euphoric scenes at Madison Square Garden, Anunoby remained calm.

"It wasn't a lot of celebration immediately because we had another game to win," he said. "We didn't want to be ahead of ourselves and celebrate prematurely."

New York completed the job in Game 5 before celebrating with a parade through the famous Canyon of Heroes, where Anunoby and his team-mates were presented with the keys to the city, a tradition for NBA champions.

"It was really cool. It was a great honour. I'm sure the whole team were all excited and all felt amazing about it," he said.

But attention has already shifted. The 29-year-old's return home comes at a significant time for the sport, with participation continuing to rise despite a turbulent period for basketball in Britain, including league restructuring and governance challenges.

While British basketball continues to search for further growth, the pathway to the NBA is becoming increasingly visible.

Tobi Lawal became the latest Brit to hear his name called in the NBA Draft this summer, joining Anunoby and Amari Williams as Brit-born players in the NBA.

Anunoby sees no reason for that progress to slow down.

"Each year more and more Brits are coming to the NBA. The game is growing each year. It's amazing to see and it's just going to keep getting better and better," he said.

The NBA itself has become increasingly international. Recent MVP awards have been dominated by players from outside the USA, while rosters across the league now regularly feature talent from around the world.

Now with Anunoby's launch into the spotlight and this year's finals performances, it seems there is more opportunity for British talent to be inspired and developed.

Anunoby believes basketball's growth is only heading in one direction. "Teams have three or four international guys now, and each year it's growing more and more. It's been amazing to see."

His commitment to British basketball extends beyond simply talking about its future. Back in London, Anunoby is once again working alongside Badu Basketball and Skechers, hosting camps designed to give young players access to elite coaching.

Watching children queue for photographs, autographs and a glimpse of the NBA champions' Larry O'Brien Trophy, it's clear the impact stretches beyond basketball drills. For many, seeing a London-born NBA champion standing in front of them makes the dream feel real.

"Every summer we do a camp," explained Anunoby. "A bunch of kids come out, boys and girls of different age ranges. We put them through drills, let them play, have a little Q&A and really just hang out with them, talk basketball and play basketball. It's a really great time."

Despite spending his time in New York, London remains a second home in more ways than one for Anunoby. An Arsenal supporter since childhood, he still follows the club closely from America.

"Just watching Arsenal as a kid and then when I moved to the States, watching Arsenal, playing with them on FIFA, just supporting from afar," he explains of his affiliation for the newly crowned Premier League champions.

Thierry Henry remains his favourite player while Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Declan Rice and Myles Lewis-Skelly are among the current squad he enjoys watching.

He even shared Arsenal's title run with then-Knicks team-mate Jeremy Sochan, another Gunners fan.

"We were always talking about it every day and I was just very excited and happy for all the guys, all the coaches, the whole organisation," he said.

Anunoby's attention is now focused on the next challenge. Indeed, his answer to what comes next could easily be shared by Mikel Arteta's Arsenal as they, like the Knicks, look to defend a title they spent decades yearning for.

"Just continue to get better individually and as a team - and hopefully win the championship all over again."

The Game 4 tip-in will continue to be replayed for years to come, but Anunoby's legacy will not just be measured by championships or iconic moments.

With his ambitions, it will also be found on basketball courts across Britain, where the next generation of players can look at a British NBA player and believe that the journey from Harlesden to NBA champion is possible.

articles.title: Caitlin Clark Drops Honest Quotes on Fever's Loss to Mystics and 'Confidence' for WNBA Playoff Run
articles.summary: Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark thought her team was "sloppy in everything we tried to execute" in Sunday's 93-77 loss to the Washington Mystics.
articles.body:
Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark thought her team was "sloppy in everything we tried to execute" in Sunday's 93-77 loss to the Washington Mystics.

The three-time All-Star also candidly described the Fever's defense as "pitiful" in her postgame press conference.

Clark credited the Mystics with playing "really beautiful basketball" offensively thanks to their movement on and off the ball.

Only one game separates the fifth-place Fever from Washington in seventh place. The teams could cross paths in the playoffs, and Clark acknowledged Sunday's outcome may not have "boosted our confidence."

"But at the same time, it's never as bad as it seems and it's never as good as it seems," she said. "We shot the ball probably as poorly as we've shot it all year long. Sometimes that's just how the game of basketball goes."

Indiana was undone by a slow start. The Mystics led 34-19 after the first quarter, and that provided them with enough cushion the rest of the way.

Forward Kiki Iriafen (21 points and 14 rebounds) and center Shakira Austin (20 points and 10 rebounds) both had double-doubles, while guard Sonia Citron was one assist away from joining them in that regard.

Clark and Kelsey Mitchell combined for 47 points but shot a combined 6-of-20 from beyond the arc. Clark also had as many turnovers as assists (five). It was just one of those days for Indy.

The Fever close out the regular season with two games against the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx, who snapped a three-game losing skid Sunday.

You'd prefer to avoid matchups that difficult because one or two losses could cause Indiana to fall in the standings. Two games are all that separate the Atlanta Dream in fourth from the Dallas Wings in eighth.

On the other hand, notching a win or even getting two straight over the Lynx could do wonders toward sending the Fever into the playoffs on a high note.

articles.title: NBA Preseason Power Rankings: How all 30 teams stack up for 2026-27
articles.summary: Here's a look at what's changed, what's exciting, and what's concerning for each team.
articles.body:
LeBron James and Jaylen Brown are in Philadelphia , Giannis Antetokounmpo is in Miami , and Kawhi Leonard is back in Toronto . But did any of these moves produce a team better than the defending champion Knicks ? Or the two best teams in the West: San Antonio and Oklahoma City ?

With the NBA season one month away, it's time for my preseason power rankings. Let's count down from 30 to 1 based on how I stack up everyone's chances of winning the NBA Finals, and look at what's changed, what's exciting, and what's concerning for each team.

What's changed: Sacramento used the seventh pick on point guard Darius Acuff Jr. and took two-time national champion Alex Karaban with the 29th pick, giving its collection of veteran scorers two young guys to develop. DeMar DeRozan left for Denver, and the Kings added Ben Simmons .

What's exciting: Sacramento has a lot of appealing young talent: Acuff, Karaban, Nique Clifford , and Maxime Raynaud. But Acuff is the headliner as an electric scorer who can shake a defender with a crossover, toss up a floater over a big, or pull up from deep. What makes him so intriguing is how much control he has over all that creativity. At 6-foot-2, Acuff uses pace to manipulate defenses, and recognizes when to hunt his own shot and when to feed a teammate. He's also comfortable working without the ball, which could allow him to play off Zach LaVine or operate out of handoffs with Domantas Sabonis . Even if the Kings aren't winning many games, Acuff could become a reason to tune in.

What's concerning: What happens if Acuff struggles as a rookie? He couldn't buy a shot during summer league and turned the ball over far too often. Point guards, especially smaller ones, are often slow starters in their careers. So if those problems carry into the regular season, what will Kings fans have to latch on to? Acuff deserves time to figure things out, but losing is easier to stomach when you can see the future taking shape.

What's changed: The Giannis era is over. Milwaukee sent Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis to Miami for Tyler Herro , Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr. , Kasparas Jakučionis and draft capital, including the pick used on Nate Ament. The Bucks also drafted Brayden Burries and hired Taylor Jenkins to replace Doc Rivers.

What's exciting: After years of chasing a second championship around one of the greatest players ever, Milwaukee has a new coach and a bunch of promising players to build around. Watching those young guys develop should be a rewarding experience for Bucks fans. The two rookies — Burries and Ament — will draw most of the attention, as will the imports from Miami. But Bucks fans know the existing roster also already had some intriguing young guys with Ryan Rollins , Ousmane Dieng and Bogoljub Marković. Last season, Rollins averaged 22.4 points per 75 possessions on 58% true shooting in minutes without Giannis, per DataBallr. So he's already shown he can handle more scoring responsibility. Now Milwaukee gets to find out whether he can become one of the players it builds around.

What's concerning: The Bucks don't own their 2027 first-round pick. It's headed to New Orleans or Atlanta. So Milwaukee has every incentive to win. But a team leaning on Herro, Myles Turner and Kyle Kuzma as its best players has a slim chance of even sniffing the play-in. Unless one of the young guys makes a significant and unexpected leap, this could feel like an aimless year with too little talent to compete, with the losses improving somebody else's draft position. For the first time in a long time, Bucks fans will have to count player development as a victory.

What's changed: Kawhi Leonard is headed to Toronto for Brandon Ingram , Gradey Dick, and a handful of first-round picks that'll help replenish what was lost in the punishment for salary-cap circumvention. Amid the fines and the suspensions, the Clippers drafted Keaton Wagler with the fifth pick, added Max Strus and Rui Hachimura , and re-signed Bradley Beal . John Collins and Bennedict Mathurin also left in free agency.

What's exciting: Can the pick-and-roll combination of Keaton Wagler and Yanic Konan Niederhäuser turn into something special? Yanic showed plenty of flashes screening for James Harden last season, exploding for lobs and showing enough coordination to catch on the move, take a dribble and finish. Wagler could give him plenty more opportunities. He was one of college basketball's best playmakers at Illinois, and together they could form a duo that gives Clippers fans something to feel good about amid a murky time in the franchise's history.

What's concerning: I feel for Clippers fans. The franchise is depleted of draft picks, and while there are young players worth watching, only Wagler offers star upside — and that's coming from a big fan of Kobe Sanders . That puts a lot of pressure on Wagler to become someone the next era can revolve around. And if he doesn't? Gulp. As a franchise, how do you sell patience when you can't offer a clear path forward? For many fans, it'll be hard to find a reason to tune in.

What's changed: New Orleans hired Jamahl Mosley to replace interim head coach James Borrego, but the most significant addition to the roster was Bennedict Mathurin. The Pelicans didn't do much else. Trendon Watford and AJ Johnson were brought in. Jordan Hawkins and Micah Peavy got sent to Memphis. But it was overall a quiet summer for a team that was constantly in rumors.

What's exciting: Jeremiah Fears is a shifty guard who averaged 30 points on 60% true shooting over his final six games. It's a tiny sample, but it helped him earn a spot on an All-Rookie team. With Trey Murphy stretching defenses, Zion Williamson pulverizing the paint, and Dejounte Murray helping run the offense, Fears has supportive pieces to help him grow. If he can continue any of the success he had to close the year, the Pelicans might translate some fun into actual wins.

What's concerning: Zion played 62 games and the Pelicans still finished 26-56. It's kind of hard to blame health for that. Fears, Zion, and Derik Queen are all at their best in the paint, so spacing could be an issue. And on defense, none is a stopper. Herb Jones and Murphy can help cover some mistakes, but not all of them. So while the individual talent is intriguing, this roster is very much composed of mismatched parts. And the front office led by Joe Dumars still has to prove it knows how to turn this collection of players into winning basketball.

What's changed: Brooklyn used the sixth pick on Mikel Brown Jr. and the 28th pick on Joshua Jefferson . Nic Claxton was sent to Chicago, but Julius Randle , Keon Ellis, and Moe Wagner were all added, so the team overall got a lot older.

What's exciting: Brown has a dangerous jumper, touch finishing with either hand, and processing speed. Though he may not be ready physically as a rookie, it's going to be fun to see what he can do playing alongside so many other talented players who can handle the ball. Egor Dëmin has size, Danny Wolf is like a point center, and Nolan Traoré brings the speed. They all create advantages in different ways, which gives Jordi Fernández plenty of combinations to experiment with. So even if the Nets aren't winning many games, it should at least be entertaining.

What's concerning: The Rockets hold Nets first-round swap rights as a result of the James Harden trade. That means the Nets have no reward waiting for them in the lottery. So Brooklyn could spend another year at the bottom without enjoying the benefits.

What's changed: Bryson Graham took over the front office, Tiago Splitter replaced Billy Donovan, and the Bulls drafted Caleb Wilson and Dailyn Swain. They also acquired Nic Claxton and signed Norman Powell as Anfernee Simons and Collin Sexton departed.

What's exciting: Wilson was the most gifted athlete in the draft, with the bounce to finish above traffic or spring back up for an offensive rebound. Then, in Las Vegas Summer League, he looked more like a go-to scorer with an ability to drain 3s off the dribble and drive to the rim. There's a chance he turns out to be the steal of the draft as the fourth pick if he sustains his skill development into real games. At a minimum, Josh Giddey should have some fun throwing him lobs, and Matas Buzelis now has a compelling frontcourt partner to grow with. Together, they give Chicago three big creators who can initiate the offense and attack in different ways. It'll be fascinating to see how Splitter gets them creating opportunities for each other as the Bulls begin to build their next era.

What's concerning: There could be a sizable gap between how exciting the Bulls look in the open floor and how difficult they are to guard in the half-court. As many shot creators as there are on the team, it remains to be seen how effective any of them will be at shooting off the dribble and thus causing the defense to respect them on the perimeter. There is a lot of pressure on Splitter to find the right combination of players to optimize the development of the young core.

What's changed: The Ja Morant era is over. Memphis traded its longtime face of the franchise to Portland for Jerami Grant and Kris Murray . The new one begins with Cam Boozer , the third pick in the draft. The Grizzlies also acquired Isaiah Stewart , drafted Karim López and Richie Saunders , signed Quinten Post, and moved Santi Aldama to Dallas. But Memphis has 19 players on contracts, with second-round pick Saunders still unsigned. At least four players must be waived or traded to reach the regular season limit of 15, so more will change in the coming weeks.

What's exciting: The Grizzlies have one of the best young cores in basketball with Boozer joining Cedric Coward , Zach Edey , Jaylen Wells , and Cam Spencer — among a long list of other talented players still on rookie-scale deals. The beauty of Boozer is he can fit with just about anyone. He can move a defender with his strength, beat him with footwork, knock down a 3 or run a pick-and-roll and fire a pass across the court. Head coach Tuomas Iisalo can use him to initiate the offense, screen for a teammate or space the floor around Edey. Memphis has plenty of young talent, and Boozer could help bring out the best in all of it.

What's concerning: Can Edey stay healthy long enough to anchor this defense? He played only 11 games last season and has undergone two surgeries on his left ankle. Foot injuries are scary for any player but especially for a center who is 7-foot-3 and weighs over 300 pounds. Last season, the Grizzlies had a 98.8 defensive rating with him and 121.2 without him, per DataBallr. Edey's size can discourage drives, force difficult finishes and end possessions with defensive rebounds. If he's on the floor, the Grizzlies could end up competing for the playoffs. Without him, they could be fighting to stay out of the relegation zone.

What's changed: Washington followed last season's trades for Trae Young and Anthony Davis by drafting AJ Dybantsa first overall. Then the Wizards kept adding veterans, acquiring Khris Middleton and Deandre Ayton while signing Young to a four-year extension.

What's exciting: Could Dybantsa end up a future MVP candidate? At 6-9, Dybantsa can devour space with long strides, stop on a dime for a pull-up, or finish through contact with either hand. Those gifts helped him lead the country with 25.5 points per game at BYU, but his developing passing makes his ceiling especially promising. When defenses loaded up on him, he increasingly found teammates with pinpoint cross-court passes. Dybantsa could become the centerpiece of a promising young core already featuring Tre Johnson , Kyshawn George and Alex Sarr. It's been a decade since Wizards fans had this much reason to dream.

What's concerning: Washington's veterans could accelerate the rebuild, but how much room they leave for the kids to develop is a legitimate question. Young and Davis will get their touches. With Middleton and Ayton also aboard, head coach Brian Keefe has plenty of experience to lean on when a game gets tight. Shouldn't the young guys be out there in those moments, though? Dybantsa needs to work through a rough stretch, George needs another chance to run pick-and-roll after a turnover, and Johnson shouldn't just be spotting up in the corner.

What's changed: After some public negotiating, head coach Steve Kerr signed an extension. Golden State also brought back Draymond Green , Kristaps Porziņġis, Al Horford , and De'Anthony Melton. Quinten Post left for Memphis, but the Warriors signed Georges Niang to add some shooting, and Brandon Williams to bring more ball-handling, and made a big investment in versatile rookie Yaxel Lendeborg.

What's exciting: Lendeborg looked like a natural fit for Golden State during NBA Summer League. As a big forward who can score from all over the floor, playmake, or cut off-ball, he brings ingredients that fit the DNA of Kerr's offense. His MVP performance in Las Vegas was an encouraging start and now we'll get to see what that versatility looks like next to Stephen Curry .

What's concerning: How much longer can the Warriors keep asking Curry to be Curry? He's 38 years old and surrounded by players with durability concerns. Draymond is 36, Horford is 40. Porziņġis has uncertain health. Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody both could miss the entire season, and even if they return there's no guarantee they immediately resemble themselves. For a franchise that's supposedly trying to make the most of Curry's remaining years, it sure seems like the Warriors are just doing a bunch of nothing.

What's changed: The Jazz surprised everyone by trading for Jaren Jackson Jr. before the trade deadline, and then they went in the opposite direction this summer by trading center Walker Kessler to the Lakers for two future firsts and two swaps. But Jusuf Nurkić was brought back and Mo Bamba and Jaxson Hayes were signed to bolster the frontcourt. Veteran wings Josh Green and Josh Okogie were also added. Most importantly, the Jazz drafted Darryn Peterson.

What's exciting: After four years of coaching tanking teams, head coach Will Hardy finally has the talent to start exploring what a winning team looks like. And with Peterson, Ace Bailey and Keyonte George , a potential Big Three could blossom in Utah. The young guys will get to grow alongside veterans with Lauri Markkanen stretching defenses, Jackson getting stops on defense, and Nurkić filling gaps on both ends.

What's concerning: Until Peterson shows he can stay on the floor, that worry will be in the back of everyone's mind following his weird freshman season at Kansas. The burst and playmaking that made him a top high school recruit never really made an appearance in college as he dealt with cramps and injuries all season. Summer League was a positive step forward. But Utah needs to find out whether he can regularly get into the paint against NBA defenders. Doing that will help determine how much offense he can create for everyone else.

What's changed: Phoenix traded Grayson Allen and Royce O'Neale for Miles Bridges , then added Luke Kennard to replenish some of the shooting it lost. The Suns also brought back Mark Williams and Collin Gillespie , and drafted Koa Peat. However, Williams will miss multiple months after surgery on a torn labrum.

What's exciting: Khaman Maluach looked like a different player in Las Vegas. He averaged 19.5 points and 12.8 rebounds while making eight of his 20 3s across four Summer League games. It's a tiny sample, but it was a vision of the versatile player the Suns hoped they were drafting with the 10th pick in 2025. Anytime a big can flush down lob dunks or pop for a 3, they offer a team an ability to play with dramatically different lineups. So if Malauch translates that success to the season, Suns head coach Jordan Ott will gain a lot of flexibility with the lineups he chooses to use.

What's concerning: Can Booker get back to superstar form? Last season, he posted his lowest effective field goal percentage since his third year. Despite his reputation as an elite shooter, he's made just 37.5% of his catch-and-shoot 3s since Chris Paul left. Booker's finishing regressed too. After shooting 63% at the rim over seven seasons, he dropped to 59% in 2024-25 and 56% in 2025-26, per Synergy Sports. Phoenix needs to find out whether this was an injury-related dip or the beginning of a decline. Booker's salary climbs from roughly $57 million this season to $69 million in 2029-30. If this is Booker's new normal, the Suns could get the supporting cast right and still be missing the superstar.

What's changed: Orlando made its biggest change on the sideline, replacing Jamahl Mosley with Spurs assistant Sean Sweeney. The roster is nearly identical, except Nikola Vučević is back in a Magic uniform as Moritz Wagner left his brother Franz to join the Nets.

What's exciting: Sweeney has worked with Giannis, Luka and Wemby. Now the highly regarded assistant gets his own team with plenty of talent to experiment with. Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner have the size to punish mismatches and the passing ability to create for teammates. Desmond Bane gives them a shooter who can also handle the ball. There are enticing possibilities in getting those three screening and cutting for each other in ways Mosley's unimaginative offense never really tapped into. With a strong group behind the stars, Sweeney has the pieces to build a team that makes opponents uncomfortable all over the court.

What's concerning: Orlando still needs more reliable shooting after finishing 27th in 3-point percentage and 22nd in 3-point attempts last season. Their two best players are part of the problem. Both Banchero and Wagner have made only 32% of 3s in their careers. Bane's shooting helped, but it wasn't enough and no additions were made this summer to address the glaring problem. Development from within will need to happen, or else it could turn into another aimless year.

What's changed: Damian Lillard will make a heroic return to Portland alongside a pretty fascinating roster. The Blazers sent Jerami Grant and Kris Murray to Memphis for Ja Morant, signed Jeremy Sochan , and re-signed Robert Williams . The Tom Dundon Owner Experience put a damper on this summer, but new head coach Micah Nori was hired and comes in with a high reputation.

What's exciting: Portland has two comeback stories to monitor with Dame and Ja. Lillard's first deep 3 is gonna cause Moda Center to explode. There really is no losing for him. As for Ja, he's got a lot to lose with only two years left on his big contract. The Blazers gave him a chance, though, and I can't wait to see how he handles it. Morant played eight games last year where he looked more like himself. If he's able to tap more into that, then the Blazers could have a dynamic backcourt duo once again.

What's concerning: On the flipside of the excitement is the worry about sacrifice. Dame, Ja, and Scoot Henderson all need touches and that's before getting to All-Star forward Deni Avdija . Are we sure a rookie head coach on a one-year-guaranteed deal is going to be able to manage all these egos and minutes? As optimistic as I am about how these guys could play together, it's undoubtedly something that could become an issue when all of them are better with the ball in their hands.

What's changed: Dallas has new decision-makers in Masai Ujiri and Mike Schmitz, and a new coach in Dusty May. The roster got younger too. The Mavericks moved on from veterans Klay Thompson and Khris Middleton, and drafted two rookies in Morez Johnson and Sergio De Larrea while acquiring Santi Aldama and Zaccharie Risacher. Kyrie Irving will also return after missing all of last season while recovering from a torn ACL.

What's exciting: Cooper Flagg averaged 25.2 points, 7.2 rebounds and 5.3 assists over his final 26 full games as a rookie — he looked like one of the 15ish best players in the league. Now if Kyrie returns and looks like Kyrie, Dallas can explore more of Flagg's versatility. One play, he'll run the pick-and-roll. Next, he'll cut inside while Kyrie creates. Irving has already thrived alongside jumbo playmakers in LeBron James and Luka Dončić, and Flagg is very much built in the same mold. Having help could reveal how much more Flagg can do.

What's concerning: Dallas ranked 26th in 3-point percentage and 27th in 3-point attempts last season, and Flagg made just 29.5% of his 3s as a rookie. Aldama and Max Christie offer some shooting, but the Mavericks need more players who can space the floor. That way driving lanes are optimized for Kyrie and Cooper.

What's changed: The LaMelo Ball era is over after the Hornets traded him to Minnesota. Miles Bridges was sent to Phoenix too. All together, the Hornets changed one-third of their roster by adding Naz Reid, Dorian Finney-Smith, Grayson Allen, Dennis Schröder, and Royce O'Neale. Coby White was also re-signed, and Hannes Steinbach and Christian Anderson were drafted.

What's exciting: The Hornets were largely dependent on LaMelo for everything before, and it led to a disastrous play-in loss. Now they have a ton of guys who can create from all over the floor, and my bet is in the long run that'll lead to far greater success. It's just a matter of who, when, and how. Could it be Brandon Miller? At 6-7, his ability to create at his size could make him a matchup nightmare for defenses. Could it be Kon Knueppel? We already know he can stroke 3s, but he's also a nifty creator. And what type of dimensions could White's downhill attacking and Reid's floor spacing provide? The combination of trading LaMelo and bringing in all these guys gives head coach Charles Lee a roster with unlimited options to create.

What's concerning: Hornets fans need to be prepared for a psychological setback. As disappointing as the play-in was for Charlotte, getting there would be an accomplishment this year. The East is far better now. There could be growing pains! And opportunities are no guarantee to immediately lead to results for the Hornets. It may take time. So Hornets fans are going to have to be patient — and new ownership is going to have to be, too, and not make any erratic decisions.

What's changed: CJ McCollum re-signed plus Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins, and Ryan Nembhard were all added. The Hawks also drafted Kingston Flemings, Zuby Ejiofor, and Henri Veesaar, so they still have young pieces after moving on from Zaccharie Risacher and Jonathan Kuminga.

What's exciting: The Hawks added enough wings and bigs that some absences in the starting lineup shouldn't wreck the rotation. Dort provides another lockdown defender next to Dyson Daniels. Wiggins is another wing scorer like Nickeil Alexander-Walker. Nembhard and Flemings can support McCollum at point guard. Onyeka Okongwu and Jalen Johnson could both take another leap forward this year, and they now have Ejiofor, Veesaar, and Jock Landale to support them in the frontcourt. With so much talented depth, head coach Quin Snyder has to be enjoying thinking up all the lineup possibilities.

What's concerning: This team is built to rack up regular-season wins, but what happens when the first action gets snuffed out? That could hold them back from becoming true contenders. McCollum scored 0.82 points per isolation with the Hawks last season, per Synergy. NAW? 0.85. Johnson? 0.78. All three of them finished below the 50th percentile. Every close game doesn't require a one-on-one bucket to win, but it sure is necessary come playoff time.

What's changed: Welcome back, Tyrese Haliburton! That's the big change after he missed all of last season with a torn Achilles. He's returning to a different roster, too, with Ivica Zubac at center, Kelly Oubre at wing, and Larry Nance Jr. at forward. Point guard Braden Smith was also drafted.

What's exciting: Aside from watching Haliburton play basketball again, I cannot wait to see how this team operates with Zubac. There's a lot of talk about how they play fast and Zubac plays slow, but I couldn't disagree more. Zubac is a quick decision-maker in two-man actions and his low-post scoring adds a brand new layer to the offense. I just can't wait to see how Pacers head coach Rick Carlisle builds layers to this offense with all his new pieces.

What's concerning: I cannot fathom what the trauma feels like for a Pacers fan. One win from a championship, and Haliburton tears his Achilles. It's just brutal. So what scares me is the thought: What if that was it? All these new additions were made, Haliburton is back, but how can I let myself feel like this team actually can go all the way? I would hope Pacers fans, and certainly the players, just use it all as fuel. Because if the Pacers do make it all the way back, and if they end up winning it all, it would be one of the most glorious feelings any sports fan has ever felt.

What's changed: Tobias Harris, Isaiah Stewart, and Caris LeVert are gone, and John Collins, Isaiah Joe, and Taurean Prince are in. The Pistons also re-signed Kevin Huerter and drafted Ebuka Okorie. But most importantly, the Jalen Duren contract situation remains unresolved.

What's exciting: The Pistons finished 17th in 3-point percentage but 29th in 3-point attempts last season, and that inability to effectively space the floor carried into the playoffs. Opponents crowded the paint for Duren and Cade Cunningham, but now the team has more shooting threats. Joe is a talented movement shooter, Prince is reliable off the catch, and Collins can knock down shots from the corners. Those additions will help out Cade on his drives, Duren on his rolls, and Ausar Thompson on his cuts.

What's concerning: The issue is that Duren returning won't necessarily mean everything is all good and dandy. Whether he accepts a long-term deal or takes the qualifying offer, the frustration from these negotiations could always linger into the season. Duren's consistency has wavered plenty of times in the past. What if that version of him returns? And even if he has another All-NBA season, we've watched him turn into a shrinking violet for two consecutive postseasons. Maybe he's just not built for it. And if he's not, then he needs to be replaced.

What's changed: After acquiring Kevin Durant last summer, the Rockets were a lot more subtle with this year's additions of Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanović. The two of them will replace Dorian Finney-Smith and Josh Okogie.

What's exciting: Houston won 52 games with Fred VanVleet missing the entire season and Steven Adams appearing in only 32 games. Their presence alone should boost the Rockets up the standings. And that's even before accounting for the development of their young players, which has to be the most exciting thought for Rockets fans. Tari Eason is still only 25. Alperen Şengün and Amen Thompson are still only 24. Jabari Smith Jr. and rookie Bruce Thornton are only 23. Reed Sheppard is only 22. This group is incredibly young, and already incredibly good. With the veterans back, if the kids get better, this team has amazing upside.

What's concerning: Last season, the Rockets shot only 36% in the last four seconds of the shot clock, per Synergy. On isolations, they ranked in the 45th percentile for scoring efficiency. Is that gonna be any better this year? Who closes games for Houston? Şengün still isn't a reliable perimeter option. Neither is Thompson. Is Ime Udoka going to resort to VanVleet chucking up 30-footers again? Will it be bully ball with Adams and Şengün crashing the boards? Or is it gonna have to be on Durant every single night? KD is 38. It can't be on him all the time, but there are no other clear answers on this team either.

What's changed: The Cavaliers re-signed James Harden, extended Donovan Mitchell, and swapped a lot of pieces around them. Max Strus, Dennis Schröder, Keon Ellis, Dean Wade, and Larry Nance Jr. are all gone. Replacing them are Peyton Watson and Mario Hezonja.

What's exciting: Harden, Mitchell, Jarrett Allen, and Evan Mobley played only 90 minutes together during the regular season last year. They barely got any reps as a unit before the playoffs began. And despite that, the team made it to the East finals. I've been plenty critical of the path there, taking 14 games to dispose of a young Raptors team and a broken Pistons team. But they still got there. With a full year together, maybe this group can develop the type of chemistry that can translate to the playoffs and lead to a championship.

What's concerning: I'm not convinced Cleveland's depth is actually any better. Watson is a solid role player, but aside from an awesome 15-game stretch last season, he was precisely just that: A solid role player! Hezonja has never shot 3s well in the NBA, so we'll see if his recent success overseas can carry over. The outgoing role players had their limitations, but they also had some clear strengths that supported the stars. And ultimately, if the stars don't get better, then this team won't be able to take the next step either.

What's changed: Kawhi Leonard is back! After a long delay thanks to the NBA's investigation into the Clippers, the Raptors officially brought back Kawhi for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, and a haul of draft picks. Veteran Kyle Anderson was also signed and the Raptors drafted Allen Graves.

What's exciting: Toronto ranked 23rd in isolation scoring and 29th in pick-and-roll scoring efficiency last season. What does Leonard do at an elite level? Run isolations and pick-and-rolls. He is an immediate solution to the biggest issue facing Toronto's half-court offense, which has to be music to the ears of Raptors fans. And to Scottie Barnes! There will be less on his plate now, which might lead to lower numbers, but should lead to a far more dynamic role. Barnes checks virtually every box on the floor as a scorer, cutter, and screener, and playing alongside Kawhi will put him in positions to excel in every single category.

What's concerning: The Raptors still need a better center than Jakob Poeltl. After ranking 26th in 3-point attempts and 21st in 3-point percentage last season, it would be ideal if the Raptors had a center who can space the floor. After all, they can only play small for so long with Barnes and Collin Murray-Boyles. Toronto has fewer draft assets after splurging on Kawhi, but finding an upgrade would boost the team's odds of making another Finals run.

What's changed: The Celtics broke up the Jays, trading Jaylen Brown to the Sixers for Paul George and draft picks. They also signed Mitchell Robinson and Mike Conley, re-signed Neemias Queta, and drafted Chris Cenac.

What's exciting: Could this be the best version of Jayson Tatum we've ever seen? There's no ambiguity that it's his team now, so it'll be fascinating to see how he handles that responsibility. But it's also possible that Tatum's usage stays close to the same and it's a committee of players that fill what's lost from Brown. Will Derrick White have a bounceback year? He forgot how to shoot last year, but he could have refound it this summer. Could Payton Pritchard take a leap? Last season, Pritchard averaged 26.7 points and 7.6 assists per 75 possessions without Brown on the floor. What will Baylor Scheierman or Hugo González look like with more chances? And could George end up having a healthy season that builds on his strong finish in Philadelphia? There are a lot of paths for the Celtics to end up even better.

What's concerning: The big concern in Boston entering last season was the center position. Even though Robinson was signed, that's still the case now. Queta had a good season but really struggled against Joel Embiid in the first round by logging 4.1 fouls in 21.7 minutes per game. Robinson is a historically injury-prone player and had his minutes managed by the Knicks. I have no concerns about Joe Mazzulla finding the best ways to replace Brown, but the center spot remains a question.

What's changed: Nuggets fans can't be too enthused with what happened this summer with Peyton Watson and Tim Hardaway Jr. both leaving in free agency. But veterans DeMar DeRozan, Tyus Jones, and Marvin Bagley III were brought in, and rookie forward Trevon Brazile was drafted in the second round.

What's exciting: The Nuggets won 54 games with Nikola Jokić appearing in 65 games, Cam Johnson in 54 games, Christian Braun in 44 games, and Aaron Gordon in 36 games. What happens if those four and Jamal Murray actually stay healthy? Murray became an All-Star for the first time and Jokić was having another MVP-caliber season before he got injured. There is a lot of doubt over the summer the Nuggets had. But the idea of what this team can be when healthy would be enough for me as a Nuggets fan to believe we can prove the whole league wrong.

What's concerning: The options behind Jokić are again pretty lackluster. The Nuggets are really comfortable with Bagley, Brazile, DaRon Holmes, and Zeke Nnaji? Really? Over the past five regular seasons combined, the Nuggets were 18.3 points per 100 possessions worse with Jokić off the floor, per DataBallr. That number will probably not be any better this year either.

What's changed: Congratulations to Pat Riley for landing his big fish! Giannis Antetokounmpo is headed to Miami along with Bobby Portis. Of course, the cost was substantial. Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez, Kasparas Jakučionis, and a pile of draft picks are gone. Norman Powell also left in free agency for Chicago. But Klay Thompson and Tim Hardaway Jr. were signed to supply shooting, and Ryan Conwell was drafted in the second round to add shot creation.

What's exciting: Erik Spoelstra must be having the time of his life this offseason imagining ways to integrate Giannis into the system. After running a unique offense last season without many on-ball or off-ball screens, I'm sure we'll see some elements of that still. But Giannis will force Miami to run more ball screens. I'm imagining Spo running big-big pick-and-rolls with Giannis and Bam Adebayo screening for each other, Klay setting slip screens for Giannis, and Giannis himself rolling down the paint after setting one for Davion Mitchell. Spoelstra is one of the best X's and O's coaches in the world, and odds are this Heat offense is going to have a long list of identities it can tap into.

What's concerning: Does Miami have enough shooting and creation? Acquiring Klay and THJ helps, but there aren't many high volume shooters on this team. And even if these guys can shoot from a standstill, there really aren't many options to take pull-up jumpers off the bounce. Will Mitchell develop it? Or will Conwell surprise everyone as a rookie? The Heat were a middling 3-point shooting team last year, and there's no guarantee it improves.

What's changed: The Lakers officially made this Luka Dončić's team. LeBron James left for the Sixers, and Deandre Ayton and Rui Hachimura departed too. But in their place the Lakers re-signed Austin Reaves, sent out a haul for center Walker Kessler, and then added Sandro Mamukelashvili, Quentin Grimes, Matisse Thybulle, Collin Sexton, and Kevon Looney. They also drafted Cameron Carr in the first round.

What's exciting: Kessler could be the best center that Luka has ever played with. Kessler sets hard screens, rolls hard, and can make quick decisions as a passer. Last season, he also began to show off a spot-up 3-pointer. Kessler is at his best on defense, though. In his career, opponents shoot only 50.6% on shots within six feet of the rim, which is 13.3% worse than their average in those situations. So he's an elite rim protector who also brings the precise offensive traits that a center for Luka would ideally have. With Kessler, more shooters on the team, and Luka in the best shape of his career, this could end up Luka's first MVP season.

What's concerning: We're gonna find out how much perimeter defenders actually matter. Dončić and Reaves obviously aren't stoppers. But neither is Mamu, Grimes, Sexton, or Jake LaRavia. Maybe Kessler will clean up everything in the paint, but what happens when he's off the floor? Can the Lakers hold up? There is no doubt about what they can become offensively, but winning a title typically requires more success on defense than what the Lakers project to offer.

What's changed: The Timberwolves shook up the whole team by getting rid of Julius Randle and Naz Reid, and bringing in LaMelo Ball and Jonathan Kuminga. The whole vibe of the team is about to change with this new supporting cast, plus Ayo Dosunmu was brought back and Trey Lyles was added to replace the departed Mike Conley and Kyle Anderson.

What's exciting: Wolves general manager Tim Connelly said in May that he'd like to get Anthony Edwards easier shots because he's such an elite shooter. That's true. Edwards made nearly 50% of his catch-and-shoot 3s last season, but it came on a low volume. Who could help out that problem? LaMelo. I'm fired up to see how this dynamic develops. Will Ant tap into his inner Steph? We've seen him add layer after layer to his game, so maybe thriving off-ball is the next step.

What's concerning: LaMelo raises Minnesota's ceiling, but he also lowers its floor. His decision-making is erratic and, until last season, he was extremely injury prone. So betting on him to be the piece that helps put Ant over the top is quite a risk. It's one worth taking, in my opinion. But that doesn't change the fact it could implode.

What's changed: Philadelphia added LeBron James and Jaylen Brown. So yeah, a couple things changed. Not only that, new Sixers team president Mike Gansey signed Anfernee Simons, Dean Wade, and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope to replace veterans Quentin Grimes and Kelly Oubre.

What's exciting: Joel Embiid has never had a better chance to win a championship, or at least get through the second round of the playoffs. LeBron is LeBron, Brown just made another All-NBA team, and Tyrese Maxey brings contagious speed and energy. What if VJ Edgecombe takes a leap in his second year too? With strong depth, the Sixers have a roster that could push for 70 wins if everything clicks. So enjoy the ride, Sixers fans.

What's concerning: Could it all be too good to be true? LeBron is about to turn 42, Jaylen wasn't even satisfied being the 1B in Boston, and Embiid gets hurt every single year. There are only so many shots to go around, so as nice as sharing sounds in the summer, it may not sound as nice during a skid midway through the year. But most of all, I'm concerned about Embiid. If he can't stay on the floor, and if the Sixers can't get stops without him, who's gonna get blamed? Obviously Embiid. And who would a new Sixers front office try to trade to fix it? Obviously Embiid. It makes logical sense if that's the way things go, but that would suck. If I'm a Philly fan, I want to win it all with Embiid. Anything else wouldn't be quite as sweet.

What's changed: The defending champions mostly kept the band together by re-signing Jose Alvarado, Landry Shamet, and Jordan Clarkson — and New York's secret, Mo Diawara, was re-signed too. But Mitchell Robinson left for Boston and Andre Drummond was brought in to replace him.

What's exciting: The one piece New York lost is Mitch, which obviously hurts. Robinson is a lob threat and a rebounder, and offers rim protection. But I'm weirdly intrigued by the possibility that the frontcourt could be better this year. For one, the Knicks finally figured out how helpful it is to play through Karl-Anthony Towns during the playoffs. I'd imagine that carries into this season. Secondly, what if Drummond actually is an upgrade? He's a better passer, decision-maker, shooter, and rebounder than Robinson. He's also not as prone to injury. Maybe Diawara also gets some minutes playing power forward next to one of the bigs. There's a chance Robinson is severely missed, but maybe the Knicks end up better.

What's concerning: The simple fact that the NBA has crowned different champions for eight-straight years is a pretty simple concern. Repeating is really, really hard. And plus, New York's dominance in the playoffs makes it easy to forget how frustrating the Knicks could be during the regular season. The offense went through stagnant stretches, the defense was up and down, and even in the first round it all felt like it would be another frustrating ending. So while a championship showed New York's upside, it wasn't too long ago we saw the downside either.

What's changed: Not a lot! The Spurs followed their Game 5 loss by adding Tobias Harris and drafting Jayden Quaintance and Tarris Reed. All the main rotation guys are back, including Harrison Barnes and Julian Champagnie.

What's exciting: Everything? I mean, the Spurs just reached the Finals with their best players all still in their infancy. Victor Wembanyama can get stronger. Dylan Harper will become even more dynamic in pick-and-rolls. Stephon Castle could become more consistent as a shooter. The Spurs were ahead of schedule even defeating Oklahoma City in May. It didn't end the way Spurs fans had hoped for, but even if one of their young guys takes a leap, it might result in a far different ending the second time around.

What's concerning: Spurs fans get annoyed with me for it, but I still wonder if there's enough shooting on the team. Castle, Harper, and De'Aaron Fox are not knockdown shooters. Harris isn't elite either. Will Carter Bryant become an elite standstill shooter? I'm doubtful. Even Wemby himself made only 34.2% of his 3s across the playoffs. But it shouldn't be on Wemby to space the floor for everyone else. The goal should be creating as many easy at-rim shots as possible for Wembanyama, whether he's catching it in the paint or dribbling from the perimeter.

What's changed: Sam Presti released a statement suggesting that their moves this summer were a "financial decision." That might be true. Lu Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins were traded for no immediate help in return. But it's also possible the Thunder are using the money as an excuse to make some systematic changes. The Thunder also drafted Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz, and they have plenty of other young players ready for minutes.

What's exciting: The Thunder lost in the West finals in part because they were worn down. Jalen Williams couldn't stay healthy and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's efficiency fell off a cliff. What could the solution be? I suspect the Thunder might want to spread the ball around more often moving forward, which would alleviate the load off SGA. JDub, Ajay Mitchell, Jared McCain, Cason Wallace, and even the rookie Stirtz can all handle the ball a bit. So can all their bigs. Shai is a two-time MVP, but maybe the next step is to share the rock more often. I could be dead wrong here, but seeing how they reload, however they do it, intrigues me most.

What's concerning: There isn't much! The Thunder are absolutely loaded. They proved last year they can withstand injuries across the roster and still rack up wins. There's no reason to believe this year will be any different. That said, part of the charm with OKC is its chemistry. The way the players all huddle after games, how they interact with Thunder sideline reporter Nick Gallo, and their goofiness online. They are a young group. But I wonder, as they mature, and as contracts become a priority for some players (such as Wallace), how will vibes change? And if they do, how does that impact the product? But on the floor, OKC has all the pieces to win the title again.

articles.title: Movistar Estudiantes arranca una nueva era: "INDESTRUCTIBLES"
articles.standfirst: El club presenta su temporada 2026-27 con un nuevo proyecto institucional y homenajea a Jayson Granger e Ignacio Triana y Vicente Olivenza
articles.summary: El club presenta su temporada 2026-27 con un nuevo proyecto institucional y homenajea a Jayson Granger e Ignacio Triana y Vicente Olivenza
articles.body: El Estu ya está en marcha. Movistar Estudiantes presentó este lunes su temporada 2026-27 en el Espacio Movistar del Edificio Telefónica de Gran Vía, en un acto que sirvió para escenificar el comienzo de una nueva etapa institucional y lanzar un mensaje que pretende acompañar al club durante todo el curso: INDESTRUCTIBLES. Jugadores y jugadoras, cuerpos técnicos, cantera, patrocinadores, instituciones, medios y aficionados se dieron cita en una presentación que quiso mirar al pasado, celebrar el presente y poner las bases del futuro. Porque el Estu cambia, pero mantiene intacta una identidad que considera irrenunciable. Uno de los momentos más emotivos de la jornada tuvo como protagonista a Jayson Granger. El uruguayo, que recientemente puso punto final a su carrera profesional, recibió el homenaje de un club que marcó para siempre su trayectoria. Llegó al Ramiro con apenas 15 años, se formó en la cantera estudiantil y debutó en la ACB con la camiseta del Estu antes de construir una extensa carrera en el baloncesto nacional e internacional. Un vídeo repasó su trayectoria y su vínculo con el club y Granger volvió a ocupar el escenario que tantas veces pisó como jugador. También hubo reconocimiento para Ignacio Triana y Vicente Olivenza, máximos accionistas de Movistar Estudiantes durante las últimas temporadas. El club quiso agradecer su etapa al frente de la entidad y su vinculación con una institución que afronta ahora un nuevo capítulo. El relevo institucional fue otro de los grandes protagonistas de la presentación. Jaime González Lasso, en representación del nuevo máximo accionista, Diego Megía, ausente en el acto, presentó las líneas de esta nueva etapa y puso en valor la identidad de Movistar Estudiantes como uno de los grandes pilares sobre los que construir el futuro. En la pista, el club afronta una temporada con tres grandes focos. Las Women in Black, con Isaac Fernández al frente, volverán a competir en la Liga Femenina Endesa. El primer equipo masculino, dirigido por Toni Ten, encara el nuevo curso con ilusión y ambición. Y el filial masculino vivirá un momento histórico con su debut en Segunda FEB, después del ascenso conseguido la pasada temporada. Los entrenadores y capitanes de los tres equipos subieron al escenario para compartir sus sensaciones y objetivos ante una campaña que vuelve a poner a la estructura deportiva del Estu ante nuevos desafíos. Si hay algo que forma parte del ADN estudiantil es la cantera. Y también tuvo su protagonismo. El club reconoció a los jugadores y jugadoras que este verano conquistaron ocho medallas internacionales con las selecciones españolas en diferentes categorías. Una nueva generación que vuelve a poner en valor una de las grandes señas de identidad del Estu: formar jugadores y jugadoras, competir al máximo nivel y mantener viva una filosofía que ha acompañado al club durante décadas. El proyecto también cuenta con el respaldo de sus patrocinadores. Movistar, HP, Fundación Jiménez Díaz del grupo Quirónsalud, Ahorramas, CaixaBank, Telepizza, MGS Seguros y PUMA continúan como empresas de referencia, mientras que Adams y Unidad Editorial se incorporan esta temporada a la familia de patrocinadores. La presentación contó además con representación institucional. Estuvieron presentes Gregorio Ramírez, director general del Ayuntamiento de Madrid; Alberto Tomé, director general de Deportes de la Comunidad de Madrid; y José Manuel Rodríguez Uribes, presidente del Consejo Superior de Deportes. Pero si hubo una palabra que sobrevoló todo el acto fue una: INDESTRUCTIBLES. El club presentó el making of de su nuevo escudo, construido con 500 kilos de acero balístico, una pieza creada como símbolo de resistencia, fortaleza e identidad. Una imagen que pretende representar lo que significa ser del Estu. Porque los golpes forman parte del camino. Pero, según el mensaje lanzado por el club, lo que hace indestructible a Movistar Estudiantes son las personas que lo forman: sus jugadores y jugadoras, la cantera, las familias, los trabajadores, los patrocinadores y una afición que lleva décadas acompañando al equipo. La fotografía conjunta de jugadores, jugadoras, cuerpos técnicos, cantera, patrocinadores e instituciones puso el punto final a la presentación. El nuevo Estu ya está en marcha. Nueva etapa, nuevos retos y un mismo sentimiento. Indestructibles.

articles.title: Jimmer Fredette Wins MVP Award At FIBA 3x3 Tournament After Ending Retirement
articles.summary: Former NBA guard Jimmer Fredette made quite a return to competition over the weekend.
articles.body:
Former NBA guard Jimmer Fredette made quite a return to competition over the weekend.

Fredette was the MVP of a two-day FIBA 3x3 tournament in Phoenix. He helped Team Miami go 5-0 and beat Amsterdam 22-16 in Sunday's final.

articles.title: Tyrese Haliburton Reacts to Knicks' NBA Title, 50 Cent Wedding Video & Hooping with Floyd Mayweather
articles.summary: Indiana Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton was happy to see the New York Knicks win the 2026 NBA Finals.
articles.body:
Indiana Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton was happy to see the New York Knicks win the 2026 NBA Finals.

Ranking 5 NBA Teams With the Worst Salary-Cap Situations 😖

"It was a weird feeling," he said of New York winning the title during an interview with Boardroom (Knicks conversation begins at 39-minute mark). "I feel like I felt every emotion. I was angry, but I was also happy. I was sad I didn't get the opportunity to compete in that."

Haliburton's Pacers stunned the Knicks in the 2025 Eastern Conference Finals after also knocking them out of the 2024 NBA playoffs. He has never hesitated to taunt the Madison Square Garden crowd, and he is one of New York's top rivals in the league.

But he also explained he was happy to see his friends succeed.

"Do I think if I was healthy and we played them that we would win? Of course," Haliburton said. "I'm an NBA player, I'm a competitor. Anyone else in my situation would say the same thing. But what they did in the playoffs was special. I don't want to put down what that was because that was crazy. The whole run from the Hawks series on was unbelievable. It was mixed feelings. The Knicks, are they our rival? Yes. But I like those guys and they are friends at the same time."

While Haliburton missed the 2025-26 season as the Knicks prevailed because he was recovering from the torn Achilles he suffered in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals, he did take an important life step this summer when he married his wife, Jade Jones.

And 50 Cent just so happened to perform at their wedding as well.

"It was special," Haliburton said (6:20 mark). "We've been able to have a cool relationship for a while because his alcohol is a sponsor for the Pacers, so I got to know him. … He was supposed to come to my wedding, he was helping me look for performers to perform at the wedding. I was thinking, if he came to the wedding and a song of his came on, he would jump on the mic."

He explained other artists were asking for $750,000 to perform for a half-hour, but 50 Cent volunteered. Haliburton didn't tell anyone, leaving it a surprise for his wedding guests.

"That's family," the Pacers guard said. "Forever I've got his back for that."

It was a full-circle moment for someone who said he had never met a "real celebrity" before he got the chance to play basketball with boxing legend Floyd Mayweather prior to reaching the NBA.

"Floyd can hoop," Haliburton said (26-minute mark). … "It was before I was in the NBA, so there was an expectation that I had to get my game off. … I did really well."

It's safe to say Haliburton's game has gotten better since then, and he will look to lead the Pacers to the NBA's mountaintop in 2026-27 after watching the rival Knicks take home the title when he was sidelined.

articles.title: Clippers Name John Gibson Interim Gov. After Steve Ballmer's NBA Suspension from Kawhi Investigation
articles.summary: With Los Angeles Clippers governor Steve Ballmer suspended from all league and team activities for one year as part of the NBA's punishment for the club's violations of salary-cap rules with Kawhi Leonard, John Gibson will step in as the new interim CEO and team governor.
articles.body:
With Los Angeles Clippers governor Steve Ballmer suspended from all league and team activities for one year as part of the NBA's punishment for the club's violations of salary-cap rules with Kawhi Leonard, John Gibson will step in as the new interim CEO and team governor.

Los Angeles released a statement Monday announcing he will start immediately and "oversee the Clippers' basketball and business operations and represent the organization on NBA governance matters."

Ranking 5 NBA Teams With the Worst Salary-Cap Situations 😖

The NBA announced earlier this month an investigation determined the Clippers engaged in "a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant rules violations" that included "violating the salary cap circumvention rules contained in the league's Collective Bargaining Agreement."

It stripped the team of five first-round draft picks and fined it $30 million in addition to the one-year suspensions for Ballmer and president of business operations Gillian Zucker. Clippers president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank was also suspended for six months.

Leonard, who was fined $700,000 as part of the punishment, was traded to the Toronto Raptors this offseason for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two unprotected first-round picks, one first-round pick swap and two second-round picks.

While Los Angeles got some draft capital in return in the Leonard trade to help make up for the picks it lost, it is still staring at an uphill battle in the Western Conference for the foreseeable future.

Gibson will be tasked with helping to keep the team competitive as it looks to put the punishments behind it.

"I am honored to take on this responsibility and grateful for the opportunity to serve an organization I have supported for many years," he said in Monday's statement. "The Clippers have talented players, coaches and staff, an extraordinary home in Intuit Dome, and passionate Clipper Nation fans who, like me, care deeply about this team. My focus will be on supporting our people, providing steady leadership and helping the organization continue moving forward."

Gibson was a trial lawyer and litigation partner prior to this opportunity, as well as a "long-time Clippers season ticket holder."

Now he is tasked with helping run the team he has supported as a fan.

articles.body:
Longtime NBA forward Nicolas Batum is officially calling it a career, revealing in a video with his son that he is retiring from the league:

Batum spent 18 seasons in the NBA and most recently suited up for the Los Angeles Clippers. He also played for the Philadelphia 76ers, Charlotte Hornets and Portland Trail Blazers.

Batum told his son that he started playing basketball in 1991 when he was two and a half years old. His father, Richard, was a professional basketball player in France, and he died during a game in front of his wife and son that same year after suffering an aneurysm.

Batum saw early success when he played on the junior French national team that won the 2004 FIBA Europe Under-16 Championship, and he was named MVP of the 2006 FIBA Europe Under-18 Championship after leading France to a gold medal. He eventually caught the NBA's attention and was selected by the Houston Rockets with the No. 25 pick in the 2008 draft before being traded to the Blazers.

Batum quickly developed a reputation as a reliable two-way wing who can impact the game on both ends of the floor. He averaged over 10 points, four rebounds and five assists in three straight seasons from 2015 to 2018 when he was with the Hornets.

Though he didn't see much playoff success, Batum was a member of the Clippers team that made it to the Western Conference Finals in 2021 before losing to the Phoenix Suns in six games.

In addition to his retirement from the NBA, Batum told his son that his career with the French national team is also over. The 37-year-old said he's looking forward to the next chapter of his life and the opportunity to spend more time with his family.

articles.title: Nico Batum anuncia su retirada
articles.standfirst: El alero, uno de los mejores jugadores en la historia del baloncesto francés, se despide después de 18 temporadas en la NBA
articles.summary: El alero, uno de los mejores jugadores en la historia del baloncesto francés, se despide después de 18 temporadas en la NBA
articles.body: El alero francés Nicolas Batum, campeón del Eurobasket con Francia en 2013 y con un bagaje de 18 temporadas en la NBA, puso punto y final a su carrera en el baloncesto profesional a los 37 años. Tras una carrera de 20 años como jugador, el galo explicó su decisión a través de un vídeo que hizo público este lunes en sus redes sociales, en el que apareció junto a su hijo, y en el que recordó varias de las mejores experiencias de su trayectoria. "No me asusta dejar de ser jugador de baloncesto porque he vivido todo lo que tenía que vivir. He hecho todo lo que tenía que hacer. Quizá por eso me siento tan orgulloso. Hoy soy feliz", afirmó. En su despedida, tuvo también un bonito recuerdo para su padre, Richard, jugador de baloncesto, que falleció en 1991 mientras jugaba un partido a causa de una aneurisma. Batum debutó como profesional en el año 2006 en las filas del Le Mans de su país, donde permaneció hasta el 2008. En el verano de ese año fue elegido en el puesto 25 del Draft de la NBA de 2008 por los Houston Rockets, aunque fue traspasado a los Portland Trail Blazers. Con la franquicia de Oregón jugó siete temporadas, con un breve paso por el Nancy francés durante el 'lockout' del 2011, antes de comenzar un periplo que le llevó a vestir también las camisetas de los Charlotte Hornets (2015-2020), Los Angeles Clippers (2020-2023), los Philadelphia 76ers (2023-2024) y Los Angeles Clippers (2024-2026). El jugador había permanecido sin equipo desde este verano, y hace dos, anunció también su retiro de la selección francesa. Con el equipo nacional, consiguió el oro en el Eurobasket de 2013, la plata en el de 2011 y el bronce en el de 2015. También fue bronce en el Mundial de 2014 y en el de 2019. A nivel olímpico, ganó una plata en los Juegos de Tokio 2020 y en los de París 2024, su última competición internacional. En total, siete medallas que le aúpan como uno de los referentes del baloncesto francés en los últimos años, en los que compartió pista con leyendas como Tony Parker o Boris Diaw, siendo siempre pieza clave para el exseleccionador Vincent Collet, con el que convivió la mayor parte de su carrera.

"I honestly can say I'm absolutely retired," he said. "I had a long run. It ended up in the (Naismith) Hall of Fame (earlier this year) and I am so thankful that I was able to coach and play as long as I did. For the first time, I can focus on giving TV my 100% attention, which I'm really looking forward to."

This will not be the first time Rivers works on the television side of the game.

He was with Turner Sports for three years in the 1990s and was also working with ESPN/ABC at the start of the 2023-24 campaign before he left to become the head coach of the Milwaukee Bucks.

"I don't take a lot of breaks in my life," he said. "I've always been around the game and this is a way of keeping me there. When you think about it, I've played, I've coached, I've been in the front office, I've done TV, I've done about everything you can do in our game. And that gives me an interesting perspective and hopefully I can share that with the viewers."

Still, he is best known for his coaching.

Rivers has coached the Orlando Magic, Boston Celtics, Los Angeles Clippers, Philadelphia 76ers and Bucks across 27 different seasons. His first season as a head coach was in 1999-00 for the Magic, and he was Milwaukee's head coach just last season.

His teams reached the playoffs in 21 of his 27 campaigns, including when he led the Celtics to the championship in 2008 and the NBA Finals again in 2010.

On Monday, Forbes unveiled its list of the 400 richest people in the United States, and multiple sports team owners made the cut.

Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer topped the list of sports figures with a No. 9 overall ranking thanks to his $156.0 billion net worth. Ballmer's top spot among sports figures on the Forbes list is a much-needed taste of positivity after he received a one-year suspension following the NBA's investigation into salary cap circumvention allegations involving the former Clippers star forward Kawhi Leonard, who was traded to the Toronto Raptors. "We are complying with the penalties assessed by the league, have paid the fine and are moving forward," he said in a statement.

"It's not because the Mavericks don't love Kyrie," he reported. "They do. It's not because Kyrie doesn't love Dallas and hasn't enjoyed his experience there. He has. But they're building around a 19-year-old prodigy in Cooper Flagg. So could there come a time when it makes sense for both sides to find a contender for Kyrie to go to? These are the kind of things that people around the league will be monitoring leading up to the trade deadline."

Irving has just one more season remaining on his contract until his 2027-28 player option, so he may not be with the Mavericks for long even if they don't trade him.

And moving him for significant draft capital or young players could help the front office align the roster with Flagg's timeline as the franchise's building block. After all, Irving is 34 years old and may no longer be a prime contributor when the Mavericks are once again ready to realistically compete for a title.

Surrounding Flagg with players who are closer to his age to continue building toward the future may make the most sense for a team that is coming off two straight losing seasons.

As for Irving, he would be quite the trade addition for any team in need of backcourt help.

His resume includes a championship, a Rookie of the Year, three All-NBA selections and nine All-Star nods. He is widely considered one of the best ball-handlers in league history, and he can hit from the outside and facilitate for his teammates when additional defensive attention collapses on him.

articles.title: Pistons reportedly increase contract offer for restricted free agent Jalen Duren to 5 years, $200 million
articles.summary: Duren has declined Detroit's offers previously, seeking the max contract extension for which he became eligible after earning Third Team All-NBA honors.
articles.body:
One week before NBA teams are scheduled to open training camp, the Detroit Pistons have reportedly made an effort to get restricted free-agent center Jalen Duren to report.

After the Pistons and Duren spent the offseason at a stalemate over a reported five-year, $190 million contract proposal, the team has reportedly increased its offer to $200 million, according to multiple reports.

However, that still may not be enough to entice Duren to sign because the 6-foot-10 center is eligible for a max extension of five years and $287 million after being named Third Team All-NBA last season. Yet the Pistons are apparently unwilling to go that high and devote a portion of their salary cap to a $57 million average annual wage.

Last season, Duren averaged 19.5 points and 10.5 rebounds per game and was named to the Eastern Conference All-Star team for the first time, in addition to earning Third Team All-NBA honors.

However, his production declined notably during the playoffs, sliding to 10.8 points and 8.5 rebounds. That was perceived as one of the reasons why the top-seeded Pistons (60-22 during the regular season) lost in the second round of the NBA playoffs to the Cleveland Cavaliers .

Frustration over the Pistons' lower offer — whether from Duren himself or his representation — has resulted in the four-year veteran reportedly contemplating taking a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer and then becoming an unrestricted free agent after this season.

The risk would be considerable. If Duren suffers an injury or puts up subpar numbers, he jeopardizes a lucrative contract from the open market.

Additionally, by taking the qualifying offer then getting a four-year, $189 max contract (only Detroit can offer him more) in the offseason, Duren wouldn't make more money than the $200 million that the Pistons are reportedly currently offering. (He would max out at $198.8 million, to be exact.)

Yet Duren would be banking on the belief that a max contract awaits him in free agency. The Sacramento Kings are reportedly among the teams that have expressed a willingness to offer that deal. And two other teams, one of them the Milwaukee Bucks , have shown interest, according to The Athletic .

If Duren doesn't accept the Pistons' new contract offer — or doesn't report to training camp next week — he is almost certainly indicating that he doesn't want to play for Detroit anymore.

Hard feelings on Duren's part may have developed going back to last season, when he was eligible for a rookie-scale max extension, but the Pistons didn't extend such an offer. The team did make such an offer last week to Ausar Thompson , r eaching agreement with the forward on a five-year, $155 million extension going into his fourth NBA season.

Looking ahead to Thompson's extension has been viewed as a primary factor in Detroit not offering a larger contract to Duren. President of basketball operations Trajan Langdon may also have been saving cap room in hopes of making a blockbuster addition to the roster. (Detroit was reportedly readying to offer Austin Reaves a max contract before he re-signed with the Los Angeles Lakers .)

However, that didn't happen and several Eastern Conference rivals improved themselves dramatically in the meantime. Now, the Pistons face going into the season without any new impact players and a disgruntled burgeoning star who might leave in the offseason.
